For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

Poetry uses special forms and devices. Allegory presents a second level of meaning; alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds; allusion makes an indirect reference; assonance repeats vowel sounds; imagery creates sensory pictures; metaphor makes an implied comparison; simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; personification gives human qualities to non-human things; hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration; onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds.

More poetic devices: Assonance is the repetition of vowel sounds ('the rain in Spain'); consonance repeats consonant sounds within or at the end of words; onomatopoeia uses words that imitate sounds ('buzz', 'hiss'); imagery appeals to the senses; a symbol is an object that stands for a wider idea (a rose for love); hyperbole is deliberate exaggeration; apostrophe directly addresses an absent person, object or idea ('O Death'); oxymoron joins contradictory words ('sweet sorrow'); and paradox is a statement that seems contradictory but reveals a truth.

Example of allegory: John Bunyan's 'The Pilgrim's Progress', where the journey of Christian represents the spiritual life of a believer. Example of allusion: calling someone 'a Good Samaritan' refers to the Bible. When answering, define the term and give a short example.

A ballad is a narrative poem, often simple and song-like. An epic is a long narrative poem dealing with heroic actions. An elegy expresses grief, often for the dead. A lyric expresses personal feeling. An ode is a formal poem of praise or reflection. A sonnet is a fourteen-line poetic form. Dramatic monologue presents the speech of one character in a dramatic situation.

A ballad (folk ballad or literary ballad) usually has four-line stanzas (quatrains), a refrain, simple language, dialogue and a tragic or supernatural story, e.g. 'Sir Patrick Spens' and Keats's 'La Belle Dame Sans Merci'. An epic has a heroic central figure, a vast setting, supernatural elements and an elevated style, e.g. Homer's 'Iliad', Milton's 'Paradise Lost' and the 'Mahabharata'.

An elegy is a mournful poem for the dead, e.g. Gray's 'Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard' and Milton's 'Lycidas' (a pastoral elegy). A lyric is a short poem expressing personal feeling; an ode is an elaborate lyric addressed to someone or something (Pindaric, Horatian and irregular odes); and a sonnet has fourteen lines, either Petrarchan (octave and sestet) or Shakespearean (three quatrains and a couplet).

Blank verse is unrhymed metrical verse, commonly iambic pentameter. Free verse does not follow a fixed metre or rhyme scheme. A couplet contains two successive lines, while a heroic couplet is a pair of rhyming iambic pentameter lines. Enjambment carries a sentence beyond the end of a poetic line. Refrain is a repeated line or group of lines.

Blank verse was introduced into English by the Earl of Surrey and used by Marlowe, Shakespeare and Milton. Iambic pentameter consists of five iambs (unstressed-stressed syllables) per line, e.g. 'Shall I compare thee to a summer's day?'. Free verse was popularised by Walt Whitman and modern poets like T.S. Eliot.

Other structural terms: a heroic couplet is a pair of rhymed iambic pentameter lines (used by Pope and Dryden); a quatrain has four lines; a tercet three; a stanza is a group of lines forming a unit; metre is the pattern of stressed and unstressed syllables (iambic, trochaic, anapaestic, dactylic); and rhyme scheme is shown by letters such as abab.

sections.title: La Belle Dame Sans Merci – John Keats

blocks.text: Keats's ballad tells of a knight who meets a mysterious beautiful woman and becomes emotionally trapped by the encounter. The poem creates a dreamlike and supernatural atmosphere and explores beauty, love, enchantment, isolation and disappointment.

The poem (1819) is a literary ballad in twelve quatrains. The first three stanzas are spoken by an unnamed questioner who meets a pale, lonely knight-at-arms 'alone and palely loitering' by a lake where 'the sedge has withered' and 'no birds sing'. The rest of the poem is the knight's reply: he met a beautiful 'faery's child' in the meads, made her garlands, set her on his horse, and she fed him 'roots of relish sweet, and honey wild, and manna-dew'. She took him to her 'elfin grot', where he fell asleep and dreamed of pale kings, princes and warriors who cried 'La Belle Dame sans Merci hath thee in thrall!'. He woke on the cold hill side.

Themes: the destructive power of love and beauty, illusion versus reality, enchantment and loss, and the Romantic interest in the supernatural and medieval. The circular structure (the last stanza echoes the first) and the shortened fourth line of each stanza create a haunting effect. The title, meaning 'The Beautiful Lady Without Mercy', comes from a medieval French poem by Alain Chartier.

Diction means a writer's choice of words. An essay is a prose composition on a particular subject. Figurative language uses words beyond their literal meaning. Rhetoric concerns effective use of language. Satire uses humour, irony or ridicule to expose weakness or folly. Antithesis places contrasting ideas together.

Antithesis is the placing of contrasting ideas in balanced phrases ('To err is human, to forgive divine'). Rhetoric is the art of persuasive speaking or writing, using devices like rhetorical questions, repetition and parallelism. Satire uses humour, irony and ridicule to criticise human folly or vice; it may be Horatian (gentle) or Juvenalian (bitter).

Other prose terms include tone (the writer's attitude), style, irony, parody, anecdote and character sketch. Types of essays include periodical essays (Addison and Steele), personal essays (Charles Lamb), formal essays (Francis Bacon, the 'father of the English essay') and argumentative essays.

The essay introduces members of the Spectator Club as representative social types. Through character sketches, Steele presents different sections of eighteenth-century society. The piece is notable for observation, humour and social commentary.

'The Spectator Club' appeared in 'The Spectator' No. 2 (1711), a periodical run by Joseph Addison and Richard Steele. The club members are: Sir Roger de Coverley, a kind, slightly eccentric country gentleman representing the landed gentry; a member of the Inner Temple (a lawyer more interested in literature and the theatre than law); Sir Andrew Freeport, a merchant representing the rising commercial class and defending trade; Captain Sentry, an honest soldier; Will Honeycomb, an ageing man of fashion and ladies' man; and a clergyman of great learning and piety.

The aim of the Spectator was 'to enliven morality with wit, and to temper wit with morality'. Steele's sketches combine gentle humour with realistic characterisation and give a picture of 18th-century English society. They influenced the later development of the novel.

Drama is organised through acts and scenes. Plot is the arrangement of events; climax is the point of greatest intensity; resolution settles the main conflict. Soliloquy is a speech revealing a character's thoughts when speaking alone. Catharsis refers to the emotional effect associated with tragedy. Hamartia is an error or weakness contributing to tragic downfall, while hubris means excessive pride.

Other dramatic terms: exposition (introduction of characters and situation), rising action, falling action and denouement (final outcome), as in Freytag's pyramid. A soliloquy is a speech in which a character alone on stage reveals inner thoughts (Hamlet's 'To be or not to be'); an aside is a short remark heard by the audience but not by other characters; a monologue is a long speech by one character.

From Aristotle's 'Poetics': catharsis is the purging of the emotions of pity and fear; hamartia is the tragic flaw or error of judgement of the hero; hubris is excessive pride; peripeteia is reversal of fortune; and anagnorisis is the moment of recognition.

Comedy generally treats human weakness humorously and moves toward a favourable ending. Tragedy presents serious action involving suffering or downfall. Tragicomedy combines elements of tragedy and comedy.

Comedy types include romantic comedy (Shakespeare's 'As You Like It'), comedy of humours (Ben Jonson), comedy of manners (Congreve's 'The Way of the World'), farce and satirical comedy. Tragedy, according to Aristotle, is the imitation of a serious, complete action of a certain magnitude that arouses pity and fear and achieves catharsis. Examples: Sophocles' 'Oedipus Rex', Shakespeare's 'Hamlet', 'Macbeth', 'Othello' and 'King Lear'.

Tragicomedy mixes tragic and comic elements, usually with a serious plot that ends happily, e.g. Shakespeare's 'The Winter's Tale' and 'The Merchant of Venice'. Modern examples include Beckett's 'Waiting for Godot', called a 'tragicomedy in two acts'.

Everyman is a morality play in which the central character, Everyman, is called to face death and judgement. His worldly companions cannot finally accompany him. The play teaches that material possessions and temporary relationships cannot replace spiritual preparation and good deeds.

'Everyman' is a late 15th-century English morality play (possibly from the Dutch 'Elckerlijc'). Morality plays used allegorical characters to teach moral and religious lessons. God sends Death to summon Everyman to give an account of his life. Everyman asks Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin and Goods to accompany him, but all refuse. Good Deeds is too weak because of his sins; she introduces him to Knowledge, who leads him to Confession, where he does penance.

Then Beauty, Strength, Discretion and Five Wits join him but abandon him at the grave. Only Good Deeds goes with him to the end. The play teaches that worldly possessions and relationships cannot save a person; only good deeds, repentance and God's grace matter. Characters are personifications (allegory), and the language is simple and direct.

A novel is an extended prose fiction, while a novella is shorter and a short story is more compact. Conflict is the struggle driving the story. Foreshadowing gives hints of later events. Irony creates a contrast between appearance and reality. Point of view is the position from which a story is told. Symbolism gives objects, characters or events additional meanings.

Characterisation can be direct (the narrator tells us about the character) or indirect (through actions, speech and thoughts). E.M. Forster distinguished flat characters (simple, built around one idea) and round characters (complex, capable of surprising). The protagonist is the main character; the antagonist opposes him.

Point of view may be first-person (narrator is a character, 'I'), third-person limited, third-person omniscient (all-knowing narrator) or second-person. Foreshadowing hints at future events. Irony may be verbal, situational or dramatic. Setting is the time and place of the story. A symbol is an object or event with deeper meaning.

Animal Farm is an allegorical political novel about farm animals who rebel against human rule but eventually experience another form of oppression. The work explores power, revolution, propaganda, corruption of ideals and the manipulation of language.

Published in 1945, the novel is an allegory of the Russian Revolution of 1917 and the rise of Stalin. Old Major (Lenin/Marx) inspires the animals with a dream of freedom; after his death, the animals of Manor Farm, led by the pigs Snowball (Trotsky) and Napoleon (Stalin), overthrow the farmer Mr. Jones (the Tsar) and rename it Animal Farm. They adopt the Seven Commandments, summarised as 'Four legs good, two legs bad'.

Napoleon uses his dogs (secret police) to expel Snowball, and Squealer (propaganda) twists the truth. Boxer, the hard-working horse ('I will work harder'), represents the loyal working class and is finally sold to the knacker. The commandments are secretly changed until only one remains: 'All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others.' In the end, the pigs walk on two legs and become indistinguishable from humans. Themes: corruption of power, propaganda, betrayal of revolutionary ideals and totalitarianism.

sections.title: Poetry: Literary Terms and La Belle Dame Sans Merci

blocks.text:
Poetry uses forms, sound patterns and figures of speech to create meaning. Devices such as metaphor, simile, personification, imagery, alliteration, assonance, symbol and hyperbole make language more expressive. Poetic forms include ballad, epic, elegy, lyric, ode and sonnet, while structures such as blank verse, free verse, couplet, rhyme, metre and stanza organise poetic expression.

John Keats's La Belle Dame Sans Merci is a ballad centred on a knight's encounter with a mysterious woman. Its medieval and supernatural setting creates an atmosphere of beauty and danger. The knight's final isolation suggests themes of enchantment, unfulfilled love and the destructive power of illusion.

Poetic devices and forms: Figures of speech such as simile, metaphor, personification, apostrophe, hyperbole, oxymoron and paradox add depth; sound devices such as alliteration, assonance, rhyme and onomatopoeia create music; imagery and symbolism appeal to the senses and suggest wider meanings. Forms include the ballad, epic, elegy, lyric, ode and sonnet. Structures include blank verse, free verse, couplets, quatrains and various metres.

La Belle Dame Sans Merci - summary: A speaker meets a pale, lonely knight in a desolate landscape in late autumn. The knight explains that he met a beautiful fairy lady, fell in love, and was taken to her elfin grot, where he dreamed of pale kings and warriors who warned that the lady had enslaved them too. He awoke alone on the cold hill side, still haunted.

Themes and techniques: The poem explores the fatal attraction of beauty, the dangers of romantic obsession, the conflict between dream and reality, and the sense of loss and desolation. It uses the ballad form with a question-and-answer structure, a shortened last line in each stanza, medieval setting, supernatural elements, symbolism (withered sedge, silent birds) and a circular ending.

Critical note: Some critics read the lady as a symbol of the poet's muse, of love, or even of death and disease (Keats was suffering and in love with Fanny Brawne). The poem is one of the best examples of the Romantic revival of the ballad.

Prose writing uses important devices such as diction, antithesis, figurative language, rhetoric and satire. The essay is a flexible prose form through which writers can discuss society, character, ideas or experience.

Richard Steele's The Spectator Club introduces a group of characters who represent different parts of society. The character sketches allow Steele to observe manners and social behaviour with humour. The work is useful for understanding how periodical essays combined entertainment with social commentary.

Prose devices: Diction, tone, antithesis, figurative language, rhetoric and satire shape the effect of prose. The essay is a flexible form - periodical, personal, formal or argumentative - used by Bacon, Addison, Steele, Lamb and others.

The Spectator Club - background: Steele and Addison's 'The Spectator' (1711-12) was a daily periodical that aimed to improve manners and morals in an entertaining way. In No. 2, Steele introduces the members of the club that supposedly produced the paper.

Characters: Sir Roger de Coverley (a good-natured country squire, eccentric but kind), the Templar (a lawyer devoted to literature and the stage), Sir Andrew Freeport (a successful, sensible merchant who praises trade), Captain Sentry (a modest, brave soldier), Will Honeycomb (an ageing fashionable gentleman) and a learned, devout clergyman. Together they represent the landed gentry, law, commerce, army, fashionable society and the church.

Significance: The sketches combine humour, gentle satire and realism, reflect the social life of early 18th-century England and mark an important stage in the development of the English essay and character writing, preparing the way for the novel.

Drama presents action through characters, dialogue, plot, setting, acts and scenes. Terms such as climax, resolution, soliloquy, catharsis, hamartia and hubris help explain dramatic structure and tragedy. Comedy, tragedy and tragicomedy represent major dramatic forms.

Everyman is a morality play built around the journey of a representative human being toward death and judgement. When Everyman seeks companionship, worldly attachments prove unable to give permanent support. The play uses personified figures and religious allegory to teach the importance of moral and spiritual preparation.

Drama terms: Drama is divided into acts and scenes and follows a plot structure of exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Soliloquy and aside reveal inner thoughts. Aristotle's concepts of catharsis, hamartia, hubris, peripeteia and anagnorisis explain tragedy.

Forms: Comedy deals with human follies and ends happily (romantic comedy, comedy of manners, farce); tragedy presents the fall of a noble hero through a flaw and evokes pity and fear; tragicomedy mixes both.

Everyman - summary and allegory: God sends Death to summon Everyman. Fellowship, Kindred, Cousin and Goods desert him; Good Deeds, weakened by his sins, is revived through Knowledge and Confession. Beauty, Strength, Discretion and Five Wits accompany him but leave at the grave; only Good Deeds goes with him to judgement, and an Angel receives his soul.

Themes and significance: The play teaches the transience of worldly things, the importance of good deeds, repentance and divine grace. It is the best-known English morality play, using personified abstractions, simple verse and a clear moral message, and it links medieval religious drama with the later development of English drama.

Fiction includes the novel, novella and short story. Important elements include plot, conflict, characterization, setting, point of view, foreshadowing, irony, narrative technique and symbolism.

George Orwell's Animal Farm uses animals and events on a farm as political allegory. A rebellion begins with hopes of equality, but power gradually becomes concentrated in a new ruling group. Through propaganda, altered rules and manipulation, the original ideals are weakened. The novel is therefore a study of power, corruption and the danger of political language being used to control truth.

Fiction terms: Novel, novella and short story differ in length and complexity. Elements of fiction include plot, conflict (man vs man, nature, society, self), characterisation (flat and round characters), setting, point of view, foreshadowing, irony and symbolism.

Animal Farm - plot: Inspired by Old Major's dream, the animals rebel against Mr. Jones. The pigs take leadership; Snowball and Napoleon quarrel over the windmill; Napoleon expels Snowball with his dogs and becomes a dictator. Squealer's propaganda justifies every abuse, the commandments are altered, Boxer is betrayed, and the pigs finally become like the humans they replaced.

Allegory: Old Major represents Marx/Lenin, Napoleon Stalin, Snowball Trotsky, Squealer the propaganda machine, the dogs the secret police, Boxer the working class, Moses the raven organised religion, and Mr. Jones the Tsar. The windmill stands for Stalin's Five-Year Plans.

Themes and style: The novel shows how revolutions can be betrayed, how power corrupts, how language is manipulated for control, and how ignorance and blind loyalty allow tyranny. Orwell called it a 'fairy story', and its simple style and animal characters make its political satire powerful and universal.
The Elizabethan Age was a major period of English literary growth associated with Renaissance learning, exploration and strong development of poetry and drama.

The Elizabethan Age (1558-1603) takes its name from Queen Elizabeth I. It was a time of national pride after the defeat of the Spanish Armada (1588), voyages of discovery, the Reformation and the influence of the Italian Renaissance.

Major writers: Edmund Spenser ('The Faerie Queene', 'The Shepheardes Calendar'), Sir Philip Sidney ('Astrophel and Stella', 'An Apology for Poetry'), Christopher Marlowe ('Doctor Faustus'), William Shakespeare (plays and sonnets), the University Wits and Francis Bacon (essays). Features include the sonnet sequence, blank verse drama, pastoral poetry and a rich, experimental use of language.
The Restoration began with the return of the monarchy in 1660. Its literature is known especially for wit, satire and Restoration comedy.

The Restoration (1660-1700) began when Charles II returned from exile in France, ending the Puritan Commonwealth. Theatres, which had been closed by the Puritans in 1642, were reopened, and actresses appeared on stage for the first time.

Major writers include John Dryden (poet laureate, 'Absalom and Achitophel', 'MacFlecknoe'), John Milton ('Paradise Lost', 1667), John Bunyan ('The Pilgrim's Progress'), Samuel Butler ('Hudibras'), and dramatists William Wycherley and William Congreve. Features include heroic couplets, satire, the comedy of manners, scientific spirit (Royal Society, 1660) and French influence.
Eighteenth-century literature developed in a culture of reason, social observation, satire, journalism and the growing importance of prose and the novel.

The 18th century is often called the Neo-classical Age or the Age of Reason, including the Augustan Age (Pope, Swift, Addison, Steele) and the Age of Johnson. Writers valued order, reason, decorum, wit and imitation of classical models.

Major developments: the periodical essay (The Tatler, The Spectator), satire (Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock', Swift's 'Gulliver's Travels'), Dr. Johnson's 'Dictionary' (1755), and the rise of the novel - Defoe ('Robinson Crusoe', 'Moll Flanders'), Richardson ('Pamela'), Fielding ('Tom Jones') and Sterne. Later in the century, pre-Romantic poets like Gray and Burns appeared.

Spenser's work is a sequence of twelve pastoral eclogues corresponding to the months of the year. It uses pastoral speakers and rural settings while engaging with love, religion, poetry and contemporary concerns.

Published in 1579, 'The Shepheardes Calendar' was Spenser's first major work, dedicated to Sir Philip Sidney. It contains twelve eclogues, one for each month from January to December, with woodcut illustrations and commentary by 'E.K.'. Its main character is the shepherd Colin Clout, who represents Spenser himself and suffers from unrequited love for Rosalind.

Eclogues are of three types: plaintive (complaints of love, e.g. January and December), recreative (songs and contests, e.g. April with its praise of Queen Elizabeth as 'Eliza') and moral (discussions of religion and the church, e.g. May, July and September). Spenser used archaic language and varied metres. The work marked the beginning of the English literary Renaissance.
Restoration comedy is known for wit, social satire, fashionable settings, complicated relationships and criticism of upper-class manners.

Restoration comedy, also called the comedy of manners, flourished from 1660 to about 1710. Major dramatists include George Etherege ('The Man of Mode'), William Wycherley ('The Country Wife'), William Congreve ('Love for Love', 'The Way of the World'), Vanbrugh and Farquhar.

Features: witty dialogue and repartee, intrigue and complicated plots, characters from fashionable London society (fops, wits, rakes, jealous husbands, coquettes), themes of love, marriage, money and reputation, and a cynical view of morality. Jeremy Collier attacked its immorality in 1698, leading to a decline and the rise of sentimental comedy.

sections.title: The Way of the World – William Congreve

blocks.text: Congreve's comedy centres on love, marriage, money and social manoeuvring. Mirabell and Millamant's relationship is especially important, while the play satirises fashionable society and exposes hypocrisy and self-interest.

'The Way of the World' (1700) is considered the finest comedy of manners. Mirabell, a witty gentleman, loves Millamant, a brilliant and independent young lady. However, Millamant's aunt, Lady Wishfort, controls half of her fortune and hates Mirabell because he once pretended to court her. Mirabell plots to trick Lady Wishfort by disguising his servant Waitwell as 'Sir Rowland'.

The villains Fainall and Mrs. Marwood discover the plot and try to blackmail Lady Wishfort to gain control of her daughter Mrs. Fainall's fortune. Mirabell defeats them by producing a deed through which Mrs. Fainall had earlier transferred her property to him in trust. The famous 'proviso scene' (Act IV), in which Mirabell and Millamant set conditions for their marriage, shows a relationship based on mutual respect and equality. The play satirises greed, hypocrisy and fashionable society.

Moll Flanders follows the life of a woman who struggles for security in a society strongly shaped by money and social position. Her experiences include marriage, crime, punishment and change. The novel explores survival, morality and economic pressure.

Published in 1722, 'Moll Flanders' is a first-person picaresque novel. Moll was born in Newgate prison to a convicted mother. She is raised in a gentle family, seduced by the elder son and marries the younger. After several marriages - including one in Virginia where she discovers that her husband is her half-brother - she becomes poor and turns to theft, becoming one of the most skilful thieves in London.

She is finally caught and imprisoned in Newgate, where she repents. Her sentence of death is changed to transportation to America, where she and her Lancashire husband (Jemy) prosper as planters. Themes: the power of money, survival of a woman in a male-dominated society, crime and repentance, and individualism. Defoe's realistic details and plain style make it an important early English novel.

sections.title: Historical and Literary Background: Elizabethan, Restoration and Eighteenth Century

blocks.text:
The Elizabethan Age formed part of the English Renaissance and witnessed major literary achievement, especially in poetry and drama. Writers benefited from renewed interest in classical learning, national confidence and changing cultural life.

The Restoration began in 1660 with the return of the monarchy. Literature became strongly associated with wit, satire and sophisticated urban comedy. Restoration comedy often examined love, marriage and the manners of fashionable society.

The eighteenth century gave increasing importance to reason, social observation, prose, periodical writing and the development of the novel. Together these periods show major changes in British literary taste and form.

Elizabethan Age (1558-1603): The English Renaissance brought renewed interest in classical learning, exploration and national confidence after the defeat of the Spanish Armada. Poetry flourished with Spenser, Sidney and the sonnet sequences; drama reached great heights with Marlowe, the University Wits and Shakespeare, who used blank verse powerfully. Prose developed through Bacon's essays and Sidney's criticism.

Restoration Period (1660-1700): With the return of Charles II, theatres reopened and literature became witty, satirical and urban. Dryden dominated poetry and criticism, using the heroic couplet for satire; Milton's 'Paradise Lost' and Bunyan's 'Pilgrim's Progress' represented the Puritan spirit; Restoration comedy of manners by Etherege, Wycherley and Congreve satirised fashionable society.

Eighteenth Century: The Age of Reason valued order, decorum and classical rules. The periodical essays of Addison and Steele, the satires of Pope and Swift and the scholarship of Dr. Johnson shaped prose and poetry. The novel emerged with Defoe, Richardson, Fielding and Sterne, reflecting the rise of the middle class and interest in realistic life.
Conclusion: These periods show the movement of English literature from Renaissance imagination, through Restoration wit, to Augustan reason and the birth of the modern novel.

Edmund Spenser's The Shepheardes Calendar is organised as twelve pastoral eclogues, one for each month. Spenser uses shepherds and rural settings in the pastoral tradition, but the poems deal with more than country life.

The work includes themes of love, religion, poetry and contemporary society. Its variety of speakers and subjects demonstrates Spenser's experimentation with English poetic language and pastoral form.

Background: Published in 1579, 'The Shepheardes Calendar' introduced Spenser as a major poet and is considered the starting point of the Elizabethan literary renaissance. It follows the pastoral tradition of Theocritus, Virgil and Mantuan and is dedicated to Sir Philip Sidney.

Structure: Twelve eclogues correspond to the twelve months, tracing the life of Colin Clout from youth (spring) to age (winter). Each eclogue has a woodcut, an argument, a dialogue or song, an emblem and E.K.'s glosses.

Themes: Plaintive eclogues deal with Colin's unrequited love for Rosalind; recreative eclogues include singing contests and the April eclogue praising Queen Elizabeth as Eliza, queen of shepherds; moral eclogues discuss corruption in the church, the role of poetry and the duties of pastors.

Style and significance: Spenser experimented with metres and used archaic and rustic words to create an English poetic language. The work combined pastoral convention with contemporary religious and political comment and established Spenser's reputation as 'the poet's poet'.

William Congreve's The Way of the World is a Restoration comedy built around love, marriage, money and social intrigue. Mirabell wishes to marry Millamant, but financial and family complications create the main action.

The play is famous for witty dialogue and its satirical presentation of fashionable society. Through characters concerned with reputation, property and relationships, Congreve exposes hypocrisy and self-interest. The relationship between Mirabell and Millamant also presents marriage as something requiring negotiation and mutual understanding.

Plot: Mirabell loves Millamant, but she will lose half her fortune if she marries without the consent of her aunt, Lady Wishfort, who hates Mirabell. Mirabell has his servant Waitwell marry Foible (Lady Wishfort's maid) and disguise himself as Sir Rowland to court Lady Wishfort, intending to use the scandal to gain her consent. Fainall and his mistress Mrs. Marwood expose the plot and attempt to blackmail Lady Wishfort. Mirabell triumphs by revealing a deed of trust signed by Mrs. Fainall, protecting her fortune, and he wins Millamant.

Characters: Mirabell (witty, clever lover), Millamant (witty, independent heroine), Lady Wishfort (vain, ageing widow), Fainall (villainous, mercenary husband), Mrs. Marwood (jealous, scheming), Witwoud and Petulant (fops), and Sir Wilfull Witwoud (a country squire).

Themes: Love and marriage, money and inheritance, reputation, deception and the 'way of the world', i.e. the selfish and calculating behaviour of fashionable society. The proviso scene presents a modern idea of marriage based on mutual respect and freedom.
Style: Brilliant witty dialogue, complex plotting and satire make it the finest comedy of manners, though its complicated plot made it less popular on its first performance.

Daniel Defoe's Moll Flanders presents the life of a woman repeatedly trying to secure economic and social stability. Her life passes through marriages, financial difficulty, criminal activity and punishment before later change.

The novel reflects a world where money and social position strongly influence personal choices. Moll is both morally questionable and highly resourceful. Her story allows Defoe to explore survival, crime, repentance, individualism and the economic pressures of eighteenth-century society.

Plot: Born in Newgate, Moll grows up as a servant in a respectable family, is seduced by the elder brother and marries the younger. After his death she marries several times - including a draper, and a man in Virginia who turns out to be her half-brother - and has many children. Growing poor and older, she becomes a skilled thief in London, is finally arrested, repents in Newgate and is transported to Virginia with her husband Jemy, where they become prosperous.

Character of Moll: She is resourceful, practical, determined and calculating, but also capable of affection and repentance. Her life shows how poverty and the limited options for women pushed them into dependence on marriage or crime.
Themes: Money and economic survival, the position of women, crime and punishment, repentance and salvation (Puritan spiritual autobiography), and individualism in an emerging capitalist society.

Style and significance: Written as a first-person confession in plain, realistic prose with detailed accounts of money and objects, it is an important early English novel and a picaresque narrative that influenced later realistic fiction.
A simile makes a comparison using 'like' or 'as', while a metaphor directly describes one thing in terms of another.

Examples of simile: 'My love is like a red, red rose' (Burns); 'I wandered lonely as a cloud' (Wordsworth). Examples of metaphor: 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare); 'Life is but a walking shadow'.

A simile makes the comparison explicit and is softer; a metaphor identifies one thing with another and is stronger. An extended metaphor continues across several lines, and a mixed metaphor combines unrelated images. Both help make abstract ideas vivid and concrete.
Allusion is an indirect reference to a known person, event, story or text. Personification gives human qualities to non-human things.

Allusions may be biblical, mythological, historical or literary. Example: 'He was a Judas' (betrayal); in Eliot's 'Journey of the Magi', 'three trees on the low sky' alludes to the crucifixion. Allusions enrich meaning but require shared knowledge between poet and reader.

Personification examples: 'Death, be not proud' (Donne); 'Because I could not stop for Death - / He kindly stopped for me' (Dickinson); Keats's autumn 'sitting careless on a granary floor'. It makes abstract ideas and nature lively and emotionally close to the reader.
Alliteration repeats initial consonant sounds. Climax arranges ideas or events toward a point of greatest intensity.

Alliteration examples: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers'; 'The fair breeze blew, the white foam flew' (Coleridge). It creates rhythm, emphasis and musical effect and makes lines memorable.

Climax in rhetoric arranges words or ideas in increasing order of importance: 'I came, I saw, I conquered' (Caesar). The opposite is anticlimax or bathos, a sudden fall from the serious to the trivial, as in Pope's 'The Rape of the Lock'. In plot, the climax is the turning point of highest tension.
A lyric expresses personal emotion. A sonnet is a fourteen-line poetic form. An ode is a formal lyrical poem of praise or meditation.

Lyric: originally a song sung to the lyre, a lyric is short, personal, emotional and musical; it includes sonnets, odes, elegies and songs. Sonnet: the Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet has an octave (abbaabba) and sestet (cdecde or cdcdcd) with a turn (volta); the Shakespearean (English) sonnet has three quatrains and a couplet (abab cdcd efef gg); the Spenserian sonnet uses interlocking rhyme (abab bcbc cdcd ee).

Ode: the Pindaric ode has strophe, antistrophe and epode; the Horatian ode has regular stanzas; the irregular ode varies freely. Keats's great odes of 1819 ('Ode to a Nightingale', 'Ode on a Grecian Urn', 'To Autumn') are famous examples.
Metaphysical poetry is associated with intellectual argument, unusual comparisons or conceits and a close connection between thought and feeling.

The term 'metaphysical' was used by Dr. Johnson in his 'Life of Cowley' to describe 17th-century poets like John Donne, George Herbert, Andrew Marvell, Henry Vaughan and Richard Crashaw. T.S. Eliot later praised their 'unified sensibility'.

Features: the metaphysical conceit (far-fetched comparison, such as Donne's comparison of lovers to the legs of a compass in 'A Valediction: Forbidding Mourning'), wit, argumentative structure, colloquial and dramatic openings ('Busy old fool, unruly sun'), use of learning from science, theology and philosophy, and themes of love, religion and death.
A dramatic monologue is a poem spoken by one imagined character whose speech reveals character and situation.

Features: a single speaker who is not the poet, a silent listener whose presence is felt, a specific dramatic situation, and the gradual revelation of the speaker's character, often unintentionally. Robert Browning perfected it in 'My Last Duchess', where the Duke reveals his jealousy and cruelty while showing a portrait of his late wife.
Other examples include Tennyson's 'Ulysses' and T.S. Eliot's 'The Love Song of J. Alfred Prufrock'. It combines lyric and dramatic qualities and allows psychological depth.
Shakespeare rejects exaggerated comparisons traditionally used in love poetry. The speaker describes his mistress realistically and ends by affirming the value of genuine love.

Sonnet 130 begins: 'My mistress' eyes are nothing like the sun; / Coral is far more red than her lips' red'. The speaker says that her breasts are 'dun' rather than white like snow, her hair is like 'black wires', there are no roses in her cheeks, her breath 'reeks' compared to perfume, her voice is less pleasing than music and she 'treads on the ground' instead of walking like a goddess.

The final couplet - 'And yet, by heaven, I think my love as rare / As any she belied with false compare' - shows that his love is genuine and does not need false comparisons. The sonnet parodies the Petrarchan conventions of idealised beauty and celebrates realistic, sincere love. It follows the Shakespearean form (abab cdcd efef gg) in iambic pentameter.
Keats presents autumn through images of ripeness, harvest, warmth and gradual decline. The poem celebrates the season's beauty while quietly recognising the movement of time.

'To Autumn' (1819) has three eleven-line stanzas. Stanza 1 describes autumn as the 'season of mists and mellow fruitfulness', a friend of the sun, loading vines with fruit, swelling the gourd and filling the honeycombs. Stanza 2 personifies autumn as a harvester sitting 'careless on a granary floor', asleep in a half-reaped furrow, a gleaner, and watching the cider-press. Stanza 3 asks 'Where are the songs of Spring?' and answers that autumn has its own music - gnats, lambs, crickets, the robin and 'gathering swallows'.

The poem moves from morning to evening and from ripeness to the approach of winter. It accepts the natural cycle of growth and decline. It is rich in sensuous imagery (sight, touch, taste, sound) and is considered one of the most perfect poems in English.

sections.title: Death, be not proud – John Donne

blocks.text: Donne addresses Death directly and argues that it is not truly powerful. The poem presents death as temporary and ends with the Christian idea that death itself will finally be defeated.

'Death, be not proud' is Holy Sonnet X by John Donne, written in Petrarchan form with a Shakespearean-style couplet. The speaker uses apostrophe and personification to address Death and argues that Death is not 'mighty and dreadful'.

Arguments: rest and sleep, which are images of death, give pleasure, so death must give more; the best men go with Death to find rest; Death is a 'slave to fate, chance, kings, and desperate men' and lives with 'poison, war, and sickness'; poppies and charms can make us sleep as well. The final line - 'And death shall be no more; Death, thou shalt die' - presents the Christian belief in resurrection and eternal life. It is a fine example of metaphysical wit and paradox.

sections.title: Journey of the Magi – T. S. Eliot

blocks.text: The poem presents the difficult journey of the Magi to the birth of Christ. The journey becomes a spiritual experience involving hardship, transformation and the ending of an old way of life.

Published in 1927, soon after Eliot joined the Anglican Church, the poem is a dramatic monologue spoken by one of the Magi (wise men) in old age. It opens with words adapted from Lancelot Andrewes' sermon: 'A cold coming we had of it'. The journey was difficult - bad weather, rebellious camel men, hostile cities and unfriendly villages - and they were tempted by memories of 'summer palaces' and 'silken girls'.

Symbols foreshadow the crucifixion: 'three trees on the low sky', 'six hands at an open door dicing for pieces of silver', 'a white horse'. They found the birth 'satisfactory', but it was 'hard and bitter agony for us, like Death, our death'. After returning, they were 'no longer at ease here, in the old dispensation'. The poem shows that spiritual rebirth involves the death of the old self.

sections.title: Night of the Scorpion – Nissim Ezekiel

blocks.text: The poem recalls a mother being stung by a scorpion and the reactions of villagers and family. It contrasts traditional beliefs with rational responses and ends with the mother's selfless concern for her children.

Nissim Ezekiel (1924-2004) was a pioneer of modern Indian poetry in English. In the poem, the speaker remembers the night his mother was stung by a scorpion during heavy rain. The villagers come 'like swarms of flies', buzz the name of God, search for the scorpion with candles and lanterns, and say that each movement of the scorpion's poison would burn away sins of a previous birth.

The father, a sceptic and rationalist, tries 'every curse and blessing, powder, mixture, herb and hybrid' and even pours paraffin on the bitten toe; a holy man performs rites. After twenty hours the poison loses its sting. The mother's final words - 'Thank God the scorpion picked on me and spared my children' - show selfless maternal love. Themes: superstition versus science, community life, and a mother's love. The poem uses free verse, irony and vivid imagery.

sections.title: Because I Could Not Stop for Death – Emily Dickinson

blocks.text: Death is personified as a courteous companion who takes the speaker on a calm journey. The poem explores mortality, the passage from life and the idea of eternity.

Emily Dickinson (1830-1886), an American poet, wrote this poem around 1863. Death is personified as a polite gentleman caller who 'kindly stopped' for the speaker in a carriage, accompanied by Immortality. They drive slowly past a school where children play (childhood), fields of gazing grain (maturity) and the setting sun (old age and death).

The speaker feels the chill of the dews, dressed only in a gossamer gown, and they pause at a house that seems 'a swelling of the ground' (the grave). The last stanza reveals that centuries have passed, yet it feels shorter than the day she first guessed the horses' heads were 'toward Eternity'. Features: dashes, slant rhyme, common metre (alternating tetrameter and trimeter), calm tone and themes of death, immortality and the journey of life.

sections.title: Figures of Speech and Forms of Poetry

blocks.text:
Poetry uses figures of speech to intensify meaning. Simile and metaphor create comparison; allusion adds meaning through reference; personification humanises non-human things; alliteration creates sound effects; climax builds intensity.

Major forms include lyric, sonnet and ode. Metaphysical poetry combines intellectual argument with striking imagery, while dramatic monologue presents the speech of a single character. Knowing these forms and devices helps students interpret how a poem creates meaning.

Figures of speech: Simile and metaphor create comparisons; allusion enriches meaning through references to known stories; personification gives life to abstract ideas and nature; alliteration creates musical effect; climax arranges ideas in increasing intensity. Other devices include imagery, symbolism, hyperbole, paradox and apostrophe.

Lyric, sonnet and ode: The lyric expresses personal emotion; the sonnet is a fourteen-line form in Petrarchan, Shakespearean and Spenserian varieties; the ode is a serious, elaborate lyric often addressed to a person or object, in Pindaric, Horatian or irregular forms.
Metaphysical poetry: Donne and his followers used conceits, wit, argument, colloquial language and learned imagery to explore love and religion, uniting thought and feeling.

Dramatic monologue: Developed by Browning and used by Tennyson and Eliot, it presents a single speaker addressing a silent listener and reveals character and situation. Understanding these devices and forms helps students analyse prescribed poems and write strong critical answers.

Shakespeare's Sonnet 130 challenges artificial praise in conventional love poetry and values genuine affection. Keats's Ode to Autumn celebrates the richness of autumn through sensuous natural imagery while recognising change and decline.

John Donne's Death, be not proud directly challenges Death and reduces its apparent power. Its argument moves toward spiritual victory over mortality. The three poems demonstrate different uses of poetic form, imagery and argument.

Shakespeare's Sonnet 130: It is an anti-Petrarchan sonnet that rejects conventional exaggerations of beauty - eyes like the sun, lips like coral, cheeks like roses - and describes the mistress realistically. The couplet asserts that his love is as rare as any woman praised with false comparisons, celebrating sincere love over flattery.

Keats's 'To Autumn': Through three stanzas, Keats presents autumn's ripeness, its personification as a harvester and gleaner, and its own music in the evening. The poem progresses from abundance to quiet decline, accepting the cycle of life and death, and is rich in sensuous imagery.

Donne's 'Death, be not proud': Addressing Death directly, Donne argues logically that Death is not powerful but a slave to fate and chance, merely a short sleep before eternal life. The paradoxical conclusion, 'Death, thou shalt die', expresses Christian faith in resurrection.

Comparison: Shakespeare uses wit to redefine love, Keats uses imagery to celebrate nature and transience, and Donne uses argument to defeat death. All three show mastery of form - the sonnet and the ode - and deal with universal themes of beauty, time and mortality.

T. S. Eliot's Journey of the Magi presents a physical journey that becomes a difficult spiritual transformation. Nissim Ezekiel's Night of the Scorpion depicts a family crisis while placing superstition, community belief and rational thought side by side.

Emily Dickinson's Because I Could Not Stop for Death personifies Death as a calm companion. The journey passes familiar stages of life and moves toward eternity. Each poem uses a personal or dramatic situation to explore larger questions of belief, suffering and mortality.

Eliot's 'Journey of the Magi': A dramatic monologue by one of the wise men recalling the hard journey to Bethlehem, the symbolic images foreshadowing the crucifixion, and the feeling that the birth was also a death of their old way of life. It explores spiritual conversion and alienation.

Ezekiel's 'Night of the Scorpion': The poet remembers his mother's suffering after a scorpion sting, the villagers' superstitious prayers and theories about karma, the father's rationalism mixed with desperation, and the mother's selfless words at the end. It contrasts superstition and reason and celebrates maternal love, in an Indian setting with ironic detachment.

Dickinson's 'Because I Could Not Stop for Death': Death, a courteous gentleman, takes the speaker on a carriage ride past scenes representing the stages of life to the grave and towards eternity. The calm tone, personification and dashes express her unique view of death as a passage rather than an end.

Comparison: Each poem presents a journey - spiritual (Eliot), domestic and emotional (Ezekiel) and from life to eternity (Dickinson) - and uses a personal or dramatic voice to reflect on faith, suffering and mortality across British, Indian and American contexts.
Communication is the process of sending and receiving information, ideas or feelings so that meaning is shared.

The word 'communication' comes from the Latin 'communicare', meaning 'to share' or 'to make common'. Communication may be intrapersonal (with oneself), interpersonal (between two people), group, public and mass communication.

Its purposes include informing, persuading, instructing, entertaining and building relationships. Communication is a two-way process; it is complete only when the receiver understands the message as intended.
The process normally involves sender, message, encoding, channel, receiver, decoding and feedback.

Steps: (1) the sender has an idea; (2) the sender encodes it into words, symbols or gestures; (3) the message is transmitted through a channel (speech, letter, email, phone); (4) the receiver receives it; (5) the receiver decodes or interprets it; (6) the receiver responds with feedback.

Models include Aristotle's model (speaker, speech, audience), Shannon and Weaver's model (including noise) and Berlo's SMCR model (source, message, channel, receiver). Noise at any stage can distort the message.
Important elements are sender, message, medium or channel, receiver, feedback and the situation in which communication occurs.

Sender: the person who initiates communication. Message: the information, idea or feeling being shared. Channel or medium: the means used, such as speech, writing, telephone, email or social media. Receiver: the person or audience for whom the message is meant. Feedback: the response that shows whether the message was understood.

Context: the physical setting, social relationship, cultural background and time in which communication happens. Noise: any disturbance (physical, psychological or semantic) that interferes with communication.
Language, purpose, audience, environment, clarity, culture and relationship between participants affect communication.

Factors include: the sender's knowledge, attitude and communication skills; clarity and organisation of the message; choice of an appropriate channel; the receiver's attention, background and attitude; language and vocabulary; cultural norms; emotions; the relationship between sender and receiver; and the physical environment such as noise and seating.
Considering the purpose and audience helps the speaker or writer choose suitable tone, language and medium.
Verbal communication uses spoken or written words to convey meaning.

Oral communication includes face-to-face conversations, telephone calls, meetings, lectures, interviews and presentations. It is quick, allows immediate feedback and expresses emotion through tone, but it may be forgotten and is not easily recorded.

Written communication includes letters, emails, reports, notices, memos and essays. It provides a permanent record, allows careful planning and can reach many people, but it takes time and feedback is delayed. Good verbal communication follows the 7 Cs: clarity, conciseness, concreteness, correctness, consideration, completeness and courtesy.
Non-verbal communication uses facial expression, gesture, posture, eye contact, appearance and other signals without depending entirely on words.

Types of non-verbal communication: kinesics (body movements, gestures, posture, facial expressions), oculesics (eye contact), proxemics (use of space and distance), haptics (touch), chronemics (use of time), paralanguage (tone, pitch, pace, pauses) and appearance (dress, grooming). Albert Mehrabian's research suggests that much of the emotional meaning of a message comes from tone and body language.
Non-verbal cues may reinforce, contradict, substitute or regulate verbal messages. They vary across cultures, so awareness is important in intercultural communication.
Barriers include unclear language, noise, poor listening, assumptions, emotional tension and cultural differences.

Types of barriers: physical barriers (noise, distance, poor network); semantic barriers (jargon, ambiguous words, different meanings); psychological barriers (emotions, prejudice, lack of attention, fear); cultural barriers (different customs, values and gestures); organisational barriers (hierarchy, rigid rules); and personal barriers (poor listening, lack of confidence).
Barriers cause misunderstanding, conflict and loss of time and efficiency.
Communication improves through clear language, active listening, suitable channels, feedback and awareness of the audience.

Strategies: use simple, clear and precise language; know the audience; choose the right medium; organise ideas logically; listen actively (pay attention, avoid interrupting, ask questions, paraphrase); seek and give feedback; control emotions; be sensitive to cultural differences; use non-verbal cues consistently; and reduce physical noise.
Following the 7 Cs of communication and practising empathy also help overcome barriers.
Effective speaking requires suitable pronunciation, pace, volume, tone, pause and clarity.

Elements of voice: pronunciation and articulation (speaking words clearly and correctly); pitch (high or low); volume (loudness appropriate to the audience and room); pace or rate (not too fast or too slow); tone (friendly, formal, enthusiastic); stress and intonation (emphasising key words and using rising and falling patterns); and pauses (to emphasise points and allow understanding).
Practice methods include reading aloud, recording one's voice, breathing exercises, tongue twisters and speaking in front of a mirror or friends.
A mock interview provides practice in answering questions, presenting oneself clearly and developing confidence before an actual interview.

Preparation for an interview: research the organisation, understand the job requirements, prepare answers to common questions (e.g. 'Tell me about yourself', strengths and weaknesses, why you want the job), prepare documents, dress formally and arrive on time.

During the interview: greet politely, maintain eye contact and good posture, listen carefully, answer clearly and honestly, give examples, avoid negative comments, ask relevant questions at the end and thank the panel. A mock interview simulates this experience, and feedback helps improve body language, content and confidence.
A seminar is an academic presentation and discussion on a selected subject and requires preparation, clear organisation and interaction.

A seminar usually involves a presenter who prepares a paper or talk on a topic, followed by questions and discussion moderated by a chairperson. It develops research, critical thinking, speaking and listening skills.

Steps: choose and research the topic, prepare an outline (introduction, main points, conclusion), prepare notes or slides, rehearse, present within the time limit, and respond to questions politely and confidently. Participants should listen attentively and contribute constructively.
A presentation communicates organised information to an audience using clear speech, structure and, when appropriate, supporting visual material.
Structure: introduction (greeting, topic, purpose, overview), body (main points with examples, data and visuals) and conclusion (summary, key message, invitation for questions).

Tips: know the audience, keep slides simple (few words, clear images), maintain eye contact, use appropriate voice and gestures, manage time, avoid reading from slides, handle questions calmly and practise in advance. Visual aids such as PowerPoint, charts and videos should support, not replace, the speaker.

Communication is successful when meaning is shared between participants. A sender develops a message, encodes it and sends it through a channel. The receiver decodes the message and may provide feedback.

The effectiveness of this process depends on language, audience, purpose, environment, clarity and social or cultural context. Feedback is especially important because it shows whether the message has been understood.
Meaning: Communication is the process of exchanging information, ideas and feelings to create shared meaning. It may be intrapersonal, interpersonal, group, public or mass communication.

Process: The sender conceives an idea, encodes it into a message, sends it through a channel, the receiver decodes it and gives feedback. Models such as Shannon-Weaver and Berlo's SMCR explain this process and the effect of noise.
Elements: Sender, message, channel, receiver, feedback, context and noise are the main elements. Each must function well for effective communication.

Factors: The sender's skills and attitudes, clarity of the message, choice of channel, the receiver's background and attention, language, culture, emotions, relationships and environment influence communication. Effective communicators consider purpose and audience and check understanding through feedback.

Verbal communication depends on spoken or written language. Non-verbal communication includes gesture, facial expression, posture, eye contact and other visible or vocal signals.

Communication may be weakened by noise, vague language, poor listening, emotional tension or misunderstanding. These barriers can be reduced through clear expression, active listening, appropriate channels and feedback.

Verbal communication: Oral communication (conversations, speeches, meetings, phone calls) is fast and allows immediate feedback; written communication (letters, emails, reports) provides a permanent record and allows careful expression. The 7 Cs guide effective verbal communication.
Non-verbal communication: Body language, facial expressions, eye contact, gestures, posture, space, touch, time and paralanguage convey attitudes and emotions and can reinforce or contradict words.
Barriers: Physical, semantic, psychological, cultural, organisational and personal barriers distort messages and cause misunderstanding.

Overcoming barriers: Using simple language, knowing the audience, choosing suitable channels, active listening, feedback, emotional control, cultural sensitivity and consistent non-verbal signals make communication effective.

sections.title: Vocal Communication, Interview, Seminar and Presentation

blocks.text:
Effective oral communication requires clear pronunciation, appropriate volume, pace, tone and pause. These vocal techniques influence how confidently and clearly a message is received.

Mock interviews help students practise responses and professional self-presentation. Seminars require organised academic explanation and discussion. Presentations require clear structure, confident delivery and attention to the audience. Regular practice improves verbal ability.
Vocal techniques: Clear pronunciation, varied pitch and intonation, appropriate volume and pace, meaningful pauses and a suitable tone make speech pleasant and persuasive.

Mock interviews: Practising interviews helps students prepare answers, improve body language, manage anxiety and present themselves professionally. Preparation, punctuality, formal dress, eye contact, honest answers and polite behaviour are essential.
Seminars: A seminar requires research on a topic, an organised paper or talk, confident presentation and constructive discussion. It develops academic and critical skills.

Presentations: A good presentation has a clear structure (introduction, body, conclusion), simple visual aids, eye contact, good voice control, time management and the ability to handle questions. Regular practice builds the confidence needed for academic and professional success.
World literature studies literary works as they circulate beyond their original national or linguistic setting. It encourages reading texts in relation to both their cultural origin and new contexts.

The idea of 'Weltliteratur' (world literature) was popularised by the German writer Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in 1827, who believed that national literature was becoming less important and that the age of world literature was beginning. Today the field includes works in translation from Africa, Asia, Latin America, Europe, Australia and the Americas.

World literature helps readers understand different cultures, compare themes such as identity, colonialism, migration, gender and faith across traditions, and see how texts change meaning when translated and read in new contexts.

sections.title: How to Read World Literature – David Damrosch

blocks.text: Damrosch's approach treats world literature not simply as a fixed list of great books but as literature that gains new meanings when it travels beyond its original culture. Reading requires attention to translation, context and reception.

David Damrosch, an American scholar, wrote 'What Is World Literature?' (2003) and 'How to Read World Literature' (2009). He defines world literature as 'all literary works that circulate beyond their culture of origin, either in translation or in their original language'. A work becomes world literature when it is actively read in a different literary system.

He argues that world literature is 'writing that gains in translation', and that it is not a fixed canon but a mode of reading. Readers should consider the original cultural context, the role of translation, and how the work speaks to their own time and place. His chapters discuss reading across time, across cultures, in translation, and in a postcolonial and global context.
The poem reflects on the disappearance of an Aboriginal ceremonial tradition. The empty site becomes a sign of cultural loss, memory and the destructive effects of colonisation.

Judith Wright (1915-2000) was an Australian poet and activist for Aboriginal rights and the environment. A bora ring is a circular ceremonial ground where Aboriginal people performed initiation rites. In the poem, the songs, dances and stories ('the song is gone; the dance is secret with the dancers in the earth') have vanished.

Only the grass, the trees and the 'grass-overgrown' ring remain; the 'hunter is gone' and the 'spear is broken'. The final stanza alludes to the guilt of the white settlers, comparing it to the 'first blood' of Cain. Themes: loss of Aboriginal culture due to colonisation, memory, guilt and the relationship between land and people.
Atwood addresses sadness directly and refuses easy romanticisation of suffering. The poem recognises emotional pain while suggesting that sadness is part of human experience.

Margaret Atwood (born 1939) is a Canadian poet and novelist ('The Handmaid's Tale'). 'A Sad Child' (1995) is addressed to 'you' - a sad child or young person. The speaker says 'You're sad because you're sad. It's psychic. It's the age. It's chemical', mocking the common explanations and remedies (seeing a shrink, taking a pill, hugging your sadness).

The speaker admits that everyone feels unloved at times and that one will never be the 'favourite child'. The ending suggests that in moments of crisis, such as an accident, we all become the same and lose the separate self ('the light that never flickers'). Themes: depression, loneliness, the search for love and the shared condition of human suffering. The tone is frank, ironic and compassionate.

sections.title: Don't Call Me Indo-Anglian – Syed Amanuddin

blocks.text: The poem resists restrictive literary labels and asserts the poet's right to an individual voice. It questions identities imposed through language, nationality and literary classification.

Syed Amanuddin (1934-2013) was an Indian poet writing in English who lived in the United States. The term 'Indo-Anglian' was used for Indian writing in English, and some critics considered it imitative or inferior.

In the poem the speaker rejects the label because it suggests he is neither fully Indian nor fully English. He asserts that his poetry expresses his own identity and that English, though a foreign language, has become his own medium. Themes: identity, language, postcolonial self-assertion, and the freedom of the poet from labels imposed by critics.

sections.title: The Christmas Tree and the Wedding – Fyodor Dostoevsky

blocks.text: The story uses a social gathering and later marriage to expose material calculation, social inequality and hypocrisy. Adult behaviour is presented critically through observation of wealth and status.

Fyodor Dostoevsky (1821-1881) was a great Russian novelist ('Crime and Punishment', 'The Brothers Karamazov'). In this short story (1848), the narrator attends a children's Christmas party. He observes Julian Mastakovich, a wealthy, important man, who learns that an eleven-year-old girl will receive a dowry of three hundred thousand roubles. He begins to calculate and flirts with the child in a disturbing way, and harshly treats a poor boy who plays with her.

Five years later, the narrator sees Julian Mastakovich marrying the girl, now sixteen, in a church; she looks sad and pale. The narrator remarks that he had calculated well. Themes: greed, exploitation of children, social hypocrisy and the power of money. The narrator's ironic tone exposes the corruption of upper-class society.

sections.title: A Cup of Tea – Katherine Mansfield

blocks.text: The story follows Rosemary Fell, a wealthy woman whose attempt at generosity is affected by jealousy and class consciousness. It examines privilege, charity, insecurity and self-interest.

Katherine Mansfield (1888-1923), a New Zealand-born modernist writer, published 'A Cup of Tea' in 1922. Rosemary Fell is rich, modern and fashionable. After visiting an antique shop and wishing to buy an expensive box, she meets a poor young girl, Miss Smith, who asks for the price of a cup of tea. Excited by the idea of being like a heroine in a novel, Rosemary takes her home.

She feeds the girl and plans to help her, but when her husband Philip says the girl is 'astonishingly pretty', Rosemary becomes jealous, gives the girl three pounds and sends her away. Later she asks Philip, 'Am I pretty?'. Themes: class difference, superficial charity, jealousy, insecurity and the position of women. Mansfield uses free indirect discourse, irony and an open ending.
The novel follows Amir and Hassan against the changing history of Afghanistan. It explores friendship, betrayal, guilt, family, social division, exile and the possibility of redemption.

Khaled Hosseini's novel (2003) is narrated by Amir, a wealthy Pashtun boy in Kabul. His loyal friend Hassan is a Hazara servant boy. After Amir wins a kite-flying tournament, Hassan runs the last cut kite for him ('For you, a thousand times over') but is assaulted by the bully Assef. Amir witnesses it but does nothing, and out of guilt he frames Hassan for theft, forcing Hassan and his father Ali to leave.

After the Soviet invasion, Amir and his father Baba flee to America. Years later, Rahim Khan calls Amir to Pakistan, saying 'There is a way to be good again', and reveals that Hassan was Amir's half-brother and has been killed by the Taliban. Amir rescues Hassan's son Sohrab from Assef and brings him to America. Themes: guilt and redemption, friendship and betrayal, father-son relationships, ethnic discrimination and the history of Afghanistan.

World literature connects texts from different cultural and national traditions. David Damrosch's approach emphasizes that a work becomes part of world literature through circulation and reading beyond its original setting.

Readers should therefore consider both the culture from which a work emerges and the new context in which it is read. Translation, comparison and reception become important. World literature helps students recognise differences between cultures while also identifying shared human experiences.

Origin of the idea: Goethe's concept of 'Weltliteratur' (1827) imagined literature as a global exchange among nations. Marx and Engels also noted that national one-sidedness was becoming impossible and a world literature was arising.

Damrosch's approach: David Damrosch defines world literature as works that circulate beyond their culture of origin, in translation or in the original. For him it is a mode of circulation and reading rather than a fixed set of masterpieces; works 'gain in translation' by entering new contexts. He emphasises reading across time and cultures, the role of translation, and awareness of both the source culture and the reader's own culture.

Importance: World literature broadens our understanding of humanity, encourages comparison of themes like colonialism, identity, migration, gender and faith, and helps break the dominance of Western or national canons. It also highlights postcolonial voices.

Challenges: Translation may lose cultural nuances; readers may misunderstand texts outside their context; and market forces may decide which texts circulate. Careful, informed reading is therefore needed.

Judith Wright's Bora Ring reflects on Aboriginal cultural loss through the image of an abandoned ceremonial place. Margaret Atwood's A Sad Child examines sadness without treating suffering as something glamorous. Syed Amanuddin's Don't Call Me Indo-Anglian challenges imposed labels and defends an independent poetic identity.

Together these poems address culture, emotion and identity from different geographical and literary contexts.

Judith Wright's 'Bora Ring': The empty ceremonial ring in the Australian landscape becomes a symbol of the destruction of Aboriginal culture after colonisation. The disappearance of songs, dances and hunters and the reference to Cain's guilt express mourning and the moral responsibility of the settlers.

Margaret Atwood's 'A Sad Child': Speaking frankly to a sad young person, the poet mocks easy explanations and cures for sadness, admits that no one is ever the 'favourite child', and suggests that suffering is part of the human condition shared by all.

Syed Amanuddin's 'Don't Call Me Indo-Anglian': The poet rejects the label imposed by critics on Indian writers in English and asserts his right to his own identity and to English as his creative medium, reflecting postcolonial concerns about language and identity.

Comparison: The three poems come from Australia, Canada and India and deal with cultural loss, emotional pain and identity. They show how poetry gives voice to marginalised peoples and personal experiences across the world.

Dostoevsky's The Christmas Tree and the Wedding exposes the way wealth and social status influence adult relationships. Its irony reveals materialism and hypocrisy beneath respectable social behaviour.

Katherine Mansfield's A Cup of Tea focuses on Rosemary Fell, whose apparent generosity toward a poor young woman becomes complicated by jealousy and insecurity. The story examines class privilege and the difference between idealised charity and actual human motives.

Dostoevsky's 'The Christmas Tree and the Wedding': At a children's party, the narrator sees the wealthy Julian Mastakovich calculate the large dowry of a young girl and begin to court her inappropriately, while he mistreats a poor boy. Five years later, he marries the girl, now sixteen and unhappy. The story exposes greed, the exploitation of children and the hypocrisy of respectable society through irony.

Mansfield's 'A Cup of Tea': Rosemary Fell, a rich and fashionable woman, brings home a poor girl to show kindness, imagining herself as a romantic heroine. When her husband praises the girl's beauty, jealousy replaces generosity, and she sends the girl away with money. The story reveals the shallowness of upper-class charity, class barriers and female insecurity.

Techniques: Dostoevsky uses a first-person observer and a time gap to create a shocking ironic ending; Mansfield uses free indirect discourse, symbolic objects (the box, the cup of tea) and an ironic final question.
Common themes: Both stories examine how money and class shape human relationships and how surface respectability hides selfishness.

Khaled Hosseini's The Kite Runner is a novel of friendship, betrayal and redemption set against political and social change in Afghanistan. Amir's relationship with Hassan forms the emotional centre of the story.

A childhood act of betrayal creates long-lasting guilt. Later exile and return give Amir an opportunity to confront the past. The novel also examines family, ethnic and class divisions, migration and the possibility of moral responsibility and redemption.

Plot: Amir, son of the wealthy Baba, betrays his loyal Hazara friend Hassan by failing to help him when he is assaulted by Assef after the kite tournament and then by framing him for theft. Amir and Baba flee to the USA after the Soviet invasion. Years later, Rahim Khan tells Amir that Hassan was his half-brother and was killed by the Taliban; Amir returns to Afghanistan, confronts Assef and rescues Hassan's son Sohrab.

Characters: Amir (guilt-ridden narrator seeking redemption), Hassan (loyal, honest and forgiving), Baba (strong, generous but hiding a secret), Assef (cruel bully and later Taliban leader), Rahim Khan (wise guide) and Sohrab (traumatised child).

Themes: Guilt, betrayal and redemption; friendship and loyalty; father-son relationships; ethnic discrimination between Pashtuns and Hazaras; the impact of war and exile; and the immigrant experience in America.

Symbols and style: The kite represents both happiness and Amir's betrayal; the pomegranate tree represents friendship; the slingshot links Hassan and Sohrab. Written in first-person narration with flashbacks, the novel brought Afghan history and culture to a global audience.
Romantic literature gave strong importance to imagination, emotion, nature, individual experience and freedom and reacted against excessive dependence on reason and formal restraint.

The Romantic Age (about 1798-1832) began with the publication of 'Lyrical Ballads' by Wordsworth and Coleridge in 1798. It was influenced by the French Revolution, Rousseau's ideas and the Industrial Revolution.

Features: love of nature, emphasis on imagination and emotion, interest in the supernatural and the medieval, love of liberty, individualism, simple language and subjects from common life. Major poets: Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley and Keats; prose writers include Charles Lamb, Hazlitt and De Quincey; novelists include Jane Austen and Walter Scott.
Victorian literature developed during major industrial, scientific and social change. Writers frequently examined morality, class, faith, social inequality and the pressures of modern life.

The Victorian Age (1837-1901) coincides with the reign of Queen Victoria. It was a period of industrial growth, colonial expansion, scientific progress (Darwin's 'On the Origin of Species', 1859), religious doubt, social reform and the growth of the middle class.

Major writers: poets Tennyson, Robert Browning, Elizabeth Barrett Browning, Matthew Arnold and the Pre-Raphaelites; novelists Charles Dickens, the Brontes, George Eliot, Thackeray and Thomas Hardy; prose writers Carlyle, Ruskin and Newman. Features include moral seriousness, realism, social criticism and the conflict between faith and science.
Twentieth-century literature reflects modern social change, war, uncertainty and experimentation in literary form and language.

The 20th century saw two World Wars, the decline of the British Empire, psychological ideas of Freud, and rapid technological change. Modernism (about 1910-1940) experimented with form and language: stream of consciousness (Virginia Woolf, James Joyce), fragmented poetry (T.S. Eliot's 'The Waste Land') and new techniques.

Other movements include war poetry (Wilfred Owen), the poetry of the 1930s (Auden), the Theatre of the Absurd (Samuel Beckett), the 'Angry Young Men' (John Osborne), postmodernism and postcolonial writing. Themes include alienation, disillusionment, loss of faith, class conflict and identity.

sections.title: Ode to the West Wind – P. B. Shelley

blocks.text: Shelley addresses the West Wind as a powerful force of destruction and renewal. He asks the wind to spread his words and ideas, linking natural change with hope for transformation.

Written in 1819 near Florence, the poem has five sections, each a sonnet made of four terza rima tercets and a couplet. In parts 1-3 the poet describes the wind's power over leaves on land (driving 'pestilence-stricken multitudes' of leaves and carrying seeds to their 'wintry bed'), clouds in the sky (the approaching storm) and waves in the sea (waking the Mediterranean). The wind is 'Destroyer and Preserver'.

In part 4 the poet wishes to be a leaf, cloud or wave carried by the wind, and cries, 'I fall upon the thorns of life! I bleed!'. In part 5 he asks the wind to make him its lyre and to scatter his words 'like ashes and sparks' among mankind, ending with the hope: 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?'. Themes: destruction and regeneration, revolution, the power of poetry, and the poet's despair and hope.

sections.title: How Do I Love Thee? – Elizabeth Barrett Browning

blocks.text: The sonnet expresses deep and lasting love through repeated attempts to measure its extent. Love is presented as spiritual, emotional and enduring.

This is Sonnet 43 from 'Sonnets from the Portuguese' (1850), written for her husband Robert Browning. It is a Petrarchan sonnet (abbaabba cdcdcd) in iambic pentameter. It begins, 'How do I love thee? Let me count the ways.'

She loves him to the depth, breadth and height her soul can reach; as quietly as everyday needs; freely, as men strive for right; purely, as they turn from praise; with the passion of old griefs and childhood faith; with 'the breath, smiles, tears, of all my life'; and if God chooses, she will love him better after death. The repetition of 'I love thee' (anaphora) builds intensity. Themes: spiritual, all-encompassing and eternal love.

sections.title: The Unknown Citizen – W. H. Auden

blocks.text: Auden's satirical poem describes an apparently ideal modern citizen through official records and statistics. It questions a society that measures conformity but ignores individual freedom and happiness.

W.H. Auden wrote the poem in 1939 after moving to the USA. It is an epitaph for a citizen identified only by a number ('JS/07 M 378'), erected by the State. Official agencies report that he was a saint in the modern sense: he served the Greater Community, worked in a factory, paid union dues, was popular with friends, bought a newspaper daily, had insurance and a radio, car and refrigerator, held the proper opinions, and had five children.

The poem ends with the ironic questions: 'Was he free? Was he happy? The question is absurd: / Had anything been wrong, we should certainly have heard.' The poem satirises a bureaucratic, conformist society that measures people by statistics and ignores individuality, freedom and happiness.

Dickens's novella follows Ebenezer Scrooge, whose encounters with supernatural visitors transform his attitude toward money, other people and social responsibility. Major themes include compassion, poverty, family and moral change.

Published in 1843, the novella is divided into five 'staves'. Ebenezer Scrooge, a miserly businessman, hates Christmas ('Bah! Humbug!') and treats his clerk Bob Cratchit badly. On Christmas Eve he is visited by the ghost of his former partner Jacob Marley, bound in chains of greed, who warns him that three spirits will visit.
