The Ghost of Christmas Past shows him his lonely childhood, his kind employer Fezziwig and his lost love Belle; the Ghost of Christmas Present shows the Cratchit family's joyful Christmas despite poverty, the sick child Tiny Tim, and the children Ignorance and Want; the Ghost of Christmas Yet to Come shows his own lonely death and Tiny Tim's death. Scrooge wakes transformed, sends a turkey to the Cratchits, raises Bob's salary and becomes 'a second father' to Tiny Tim. Themes: generosity, redemption, social responsibility and the spirit of Christmas.

sections.title: Look Back in Anger – John Osborne

blocks.text: The play centres on Jimmy Porter and his troubled relationships. It presents frustration, class tension, emotional conflict and dissatisfaction in post-war British society.

First performed in 1956, the play started the movement of the 'Angry Young Men' and 'kitchen sink drama'. It is set in a one-room flat in the Midlands. Jimmy Porter, a working-class, university-educated young man who runs a sweet stall, is married to Alison, who comes from an upper-middle-class family. His friend Cliff lives with them.

Jimmy constantly attacks Alison, her family and the establishment. Alison's friend Helena arrives, persuades Alison (who is pregnant) to leave, and then becomes Jimmy's mistress. After Alison loses her baby, she returns; Helena leaves, and Jimmy and Alison are reconciled through their 'bear and squirrel' game. Themes: class conflict, post-war disillusionment, anger, frustration, gender relations and the absence of 'good, brave causes'.

Romantic literature emphasized imagination, emotion, nature and individual freedom. Victorian literature emerged during industrial and social transformation and often engaged with class, morality, faith and social problems.

Twentieth-century literature responded to war, rapid change and modern uncertainty and often experimented with new forms and perspectives. Studying these periods together shows the changing concerns of British society and literature.

Romantic Age: Beginning with 'Lyrical Ballads' (1798), Romantic writers like Wordsworth, Coleridge, Byron, Shelley and Keats emphasised imagination, emotion, nature, liberty, the supernatural and the individual. Their poetry was a reaction against neoclassical reason and the industrial city.

Victorian Age: During Queen Victoria's reign (1837-1901), Britain experienced industrialisation, empire, scientific discovery and religious doubt. Writers like Tennyson, Browning, Arnold, Dickens, the Brontes, George Eliot and Hardy dealt with morality, social problems, class, faith and doubt, often in a realistic style.

Twentieth century: The World Wars, modern psychology and social change led to modernist experiments by Eliot, Woolf and Joyce, war poetry, the socially conscious poetry of Auden, the Theatre of the Absurd, the Angry Young Men and postmodern and postcolonial writing.
Conclusion: The movement from Romantic idealism to Victorian moral seriousness and then to modern scepticism and experimentation reflects the changing experience of British society.

Shelley's Ode to the West Wind turns a natural force into a symbol of destruction, renewal and hoped-for change. Elizabeth Barrett Browning's How Do I Love Thee? expresses love as deep, spiritual and enduring.

Auden's The Unknown Citizen uses satire to criticise a modern system that judges a person's life through statistics and conformity. These poems illustrate Romantic idealism, Victorian love poetry and modern social criticism.

Shelley's 'Ode to the West Wind': In five terza rima sonnets, Shelley describes the wind's power over leaves, clouds and waves as 'destroyer and preserver', expresses personal despair ('I fall upon the thorns of life!'), and prays that the wind will spread his revolutionary ideas. The ending, 'If Winter comes, can Spring be far behind?', expresses hope for renewal.

Elizabeth Barrett Browning's 'How Do I Love Thee?': This Petrarchan sonnet lists the ways she loves her husband - in depth, breadth, height, freely, purely, passionately and beyond death - using repetition to express spiritual and complete love.

Auden's 'The Unknown Citizen': A satirical epitaph for a model citizen described through statistics and official reports, which ends by questioning his freedom and happiness. It criticises conformity and the loss of individuality in the modern state.
Comparison: The poems show the Romantic belief in nature and the poet's mission, Victorian intensity of personal feeling, and modern irony about bureaucratic society.

Charles Dickens's A Christmas Carol tells the moral transformation of Ebenezer Scrooge. At first he is isolated, miserly and indifferent to suffering. Through encounters with the ghosts of Christmas Past, Present and Yet to Come, he is forced to reconsider his life.

The novella combines supernatural storytelling with social criticism. Poverty, generosity, family and responsibility are central themes. Scrooge's transformation suggests that individuals can change when they recognise the human consequences of selfishness.

Plot: The miserly Scrooge, visited by Marley's ghost and three spirits on Christmas Eve, sees his past (lonely childhood, Fezziwig's party, lost love Belle), the present (the poor but happy Cratchits and sick Tiny Tim, his nephew Fred's cheerful party, the children Ignorance and Want), and the future (his unmourned death and Tiny Tim's death). He wakes on Christmas morning a changed man.
Character of Scrooge: He changes from a cold, greedy, isolated man to a generous, joyful and caring person, showing that redemption is possible.

Themes and social criticism: Dickens attacks the harsh treatment of the poor in Victorian England, the Poor Law and workhouses, and promotes charity, family, kindness and the Christmas spirit. The Cratchits represent the dignity of poor families.
Style: Supernatural elements, vivid descriptions, humour, sentimentality and a clear moral message make it one of the most popular stories in English literature.

John Osborne's Look Back in Anger portrays the anger and frustration of Jimmy Porter, whose relationships with Alison and others reveal emotional and social tensions.

The play is associated with post-war dissatisfaction and questions of class, opportunity and personal frustration. Its force comes from intense dialogue and conflict rather than heroic action. Jimmy's anger reflects both private unhappiness and wider social discontent.

Plot: In a small Midlands flat, Jimmy Porter rages against his wife Alison, her upper-class family, the church and the establishment, while their friend Cliff tries to keep peace. Alison's friend Helena persuades the pregnant Alison to leave and then becomes Jimmy's mistress. Months later Alison returns after losing her baby; Helena leaves, and Jimmy and Alison reconcile through their private bear-and-squirrel game.

Character of Jimmy: Jimmy is intelligent, educated and passionate but frustrated, bitter and cruel. He represents the post-war generation who felt there were no 'good, brave causes left' and resented the class system.

Themes: Class conflict, anger and frustration of youth, the failure of post-war Britain to provide opportunities, gender relations and emotional suffering, and nostalgia for the Edwardian past (Colonel Redfern).
Significance: The play's realistic setting, raw language and anti-hero introduced 'kitchen sink' realism to the British stage and made Osborne the leading 'Angry Young Man'.
An essay is a relatively short prose composition that presents ideas, arguments, observations or reflections on a subject.

The word 'essay' comes from the French 'essai', meaning an attempt or trial, first used by Michel de Montaigne (1580). Francis Bacon is called the father of the English essay ('Of Studies', 'Of Truth').

Types of essays: descriptive, narrative, reflective, argumentative, expository, personal (Charles Lamb's 'Essays of Elia') and periodical essays (Addison and Steele). A good essay has unity, coherence, a clear introduction, body and conclusion, and a personal style.
Biography is the written account of another person's life.

A biography is based on research using letters, diaries, documents and interviews, and presents the subject's life, achievements, character and times. Boswell's 'Life of Samuel Johnson' (1791) is considered the greatest English biography.

Qualities of a good biography: accuracy, objectivity, vivid portrayal of character, interesting narration and a balance between the person's private and public life. Indian examples include biographies of Gandhi and Nehru.
Autobiography is an account of a person's life written by that person.

An autobiography is written in the first person and presents the writer's memories, experiences, struggles and reflections. Examples include Gandhi's 'The Story of My Experiments with Truth', Nehru's 'An Autobiography', and A.P.J. Abdul Kalam's 'Wings of Fire'.
A memoir is a related form that focuses on specific events or periods rather than the whole life. Autobiography may be subjective, but it gives intimate insight into the writer's mind and times.
A short story is a brief prose fiction usually focused on a limited number of characters and events.

Edgar Allan Poe described the short story as a narrative that can be read at one sitting and produces a 'single effect'. It has a limited number of characters, a single main plot, a concentrated setting and often a twist or surprise ending.
Famous short story writers include Poe, O. Henry, Guy de Maupassant, Anton Chekhov, Katherine Mansfield, R.K. Narayan, Mulk Raj Anand and Ruskin Bond.
A novella is prose fiction longer than a short story but shorter and usually less complex than a full novel.
A novella is usually between about 17,500 and 40,000 words. It has more development than a short story but focuses on a single main conflict and a limited number of characters.
Examples include Dickens's 'A Christmas Carol', Joseph Conrad's 'Heart of Darkness', George Orwell's 'Animal Farm', Hemingway's 'The Old Man and the Sea' and Kafka's 'The Metamorphosis'.
Epistolary writing presents material through letters or other forms of written correspondence.

An epistolary novel is told through letters, diary entries, emails or documents. Examples include Samuel Richardson's 'Pamela' (1740) and 'Clarissa', Bram Stoker's 'Dracula' and Alice Walker's 'The Color Purple'.

Letters as literature include Nehru's 'Letters from a Father to His Daughter' and 'Glimpses of World History'. The form creates intimacy, reveals the inner thoughts of characters and allows multiple points of view.
Nehru's letter to his daughter uses personal communication for instruction and reflection. It shows how the letter form can combine affection, education and ideas about history and the wider world.

Nehru wrote this letter on 26 October 1930 from Naini Central Prison to his daughter Indira (later Indira Gandhi) on her 13th birthday. As he could not send a material gift from prison, he sent 'something of the air and mind and spirit', which no prison walls could stop.

He says he does not want to preach or give sermons, because the best way to learn what is right is by talk and discussion. He encourages her to be a brave soldier in India's freedom struggle, to do nothing in secret and to avoid things she would want to hide, to be 'a soldier in India's service', and reminds her of Gandhiji's principles of truth and non-violence. The letter shows Nehru's affection, idealism and patriotism.

sections.title: An Astrologer's Day – R. K. Narayan

blocks.text: Narayan's short story follows an astrologer who unexpectedly meets a man connected with his hidden past. The story uses irony, suspense and a final revelation to explore fate, deception and survival.

R.K. Narayan (1906-2001) set many stories in the fictional town of Malgudi. In this story, an astrologer sits under a tamarind tree with his props - cowrie shells, a saffron turban, sacred ash and vermilion - and uses shrewd guesswork to tell fortunes. He had left his village years ago after stabbing a man named Guru Nayak in a drunken quarrel, believing he had killed him.

One evening, a stranger challenges him to answer a question. The astrologer recognises him as Guru Nayak, who is searching for the man who tried to kill him. The astrologer, disguised, tells him his attacker died under a lorry four months ago and advises him to return home. At home, he tells his wife that a great load has been lifted from him. Themes: irony, fate, guilt and the deception of astrology; the story ends with a surprise twist.

sections.title: Son of the Soil – Sebastian Zumvu

blocks.text: The syllabus prescribes Sebastian Zumvu's Son of the Soil as the third prose text. Students should study its plot, characters, setting, themes and use of prose directly from the prescribed text.

Since the prescribed text should be read directly, students should prepare notes under these headings: author background (Sebastian Zumvu as a writer connected with the North-East), plot summary in their own words, list of major and minor characters with key traits, setting (time and place), themes (for example identity, land, community or change, as found in the text), narrative point of view, important quotations, and the significance of the title.

When answering examination questions, refer to specific incidents from the prescribed reading, explain how they develop the themes and characters, and avoid relying on unverified summaries. Discussing the text with teachers and classmates is the best way to confirm details.

Prose includes many forms. An essay discusses or reflects on a subject. Biography tells the life of another person, while autobiography is written by the subject about his or her own life.

A short story presents a compact fictional narrative, whereas a novella is longer but usually more concentrated than a novel. Epistolary writing uses letters or correspondence as the main form of presentation. Understanding these forms helps students identify differences in purpose, structure and narrative method.

Essay: A short prose composition on a subject expressing the writer's thoughts, from Montaigne and Bacon to Lamb and modern essayists. Types include personal, periodical, reflective, descriptive and argumentative essays.

Biography and autobiography: Biography (e.g. Boswell's 'Life of Johnson') presents another person's life using research; autobiography (e.g. Gandhi's 'My Experiments with Truth', Kalam's 'Wings of Fire') presents the writer's own life in first person, offering intimacy but subjectivity.

Short story and novella: The short story creates a single effect with few characters and one main incident (Poe, O. Henry, Narayan); the novella is longer and more developed but still centred on one conflict ('A Christmas Carol', 'Animal Farm').

Epistolary writing: Letters and diaries used as literary form, as in Richardson's novels and Nehru's letters to Indira, create intimacy and reveal thoughts directly. Knowledge of these forms helps students understand how form shapes content in prose writing.

sections.title: A Birthday Letter and An Astrologer's Day

blocks.text:
Jawaharlal Nehru's A Birthday Letter demonstrates how a personal letter can become educational prose. The intimate form allows ideas and guidance to be communicated directly.

R. K. Narayan's An Astrologer's Day is a compact story built around suspense and irony. The astrologer's meeting with a stranger gradually reveals a hidden connection with his own past. The ending changes the reader's understanding of the character and highlights themes of fate, deception and survival.

A Birthday Letter - content: Written by Nehru from prison on Indira's 13th birthday, the letter offers ideas instead of material gifts. Nehru avoids preaching and prefers discussion, encourages Indira to think about history, freedom and service, to avoid secrecy and to act openly, and to be a brave soldier in India's freedom struggle following Gandhi's ideals.
A Birthday Letter - significance: It shows the epistolary form's ability to combine love, education and moral guidance, and reveals Nehru as a loving father and a committed nationalist.

An Astrologer's Day - content: The astrologer, who has fled his village after a youthful quarrel in which he thought he had killed Guru Nayak, works as a clever fortune-teller in a market. Guru Nayak himself appears as a client seeking revenge. The astrologer tells him that his attacker is dead and sends him home, relieved to know that he is not a murderer.

An Astrologer's Day - themes and technique: Irony, guilt, fate, the human ability to deceive and the surprise ending. Narayan's simple style, vivid description of the market and gentle humour are typical of his Malgudi stories.

Sebastian Zumvu's Son of the Soil is prescribed as a complete prose text in the syllabus. For examination preparation, students should focus on the narrative, major characters, setting, central themes and significant incidents in the prescribed text. The syllabus itself does not provide a synopsis, so these details should be learned from the assigned reading rather than guessed.

How to prepare: Read the complete prescribed text carefully at least twice. Prepare a chapter-wise or section-wise summary, a character list with qualities and relationships, and notes on setting, conflict, climax and resolution.

Themes and techniques: Identify the major themes that the text itself presents, the narrative point of view, symbols, language and style, and the relevance of the title. Note important quotations with page references.

Writing answers: Answer long questions with an introduction (author and work), body (discussion of themes, characters and incidents with examples from the text) and conclusion (significance). Since this guide does not include a verified synopsis, confirm all details from the prescribed reading and class notes.
